newsitem.title: USA: Dole says it's time for America to get angry.
newsitem.headline: Dole says it's time for America to get angry.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole declared on Friday he was fighting for America's soul as President Bill Clinton tried to add parts of the South to his growing lead.

Meanwhile Dole's campaign disclosed figures suggesting it would be heavily outspent by Clinton between now and the election on Nov. 5. According to the latest monthly reports filed with the Federal Election Commission, the Clinton campaign had $25.1 million left to spend as of Oct. 16, while the Dole campaign had $13.3 million.
It was the latest sign that the election is running away from Dole. But campaigning in Texas, the Republican nominee merely stepped up his attack against Clinton.
Addressing a rally in Houston, an angry Dole compared his presidential campaign with his service in the Second World War, when he was badly wounded.
"That was America's future and we prevailed in World War II, and now we're in another fight for the heart and soul of the United States of America," he declared.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry responded, "Bob Dole went negative on Bill Clinton and that didn't work. Now Bob Dole has gone negative on America, and that's not going to work either."

The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole had lost ground on Thursday following the disclosure that his campaign manager had made an abortive appeal to Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to drop out of the campaign.

With Election Day 11 days away, Clinton led Dole by 11 percentage points, up from 8.7 points the day before. An ABC poll put Clinton's lead at 12 points and noted Perot's support had inched up to 8 percent.
Perot rebuffed Dole's entreaty, calling it "weird and inconsequential."
An even more telling statistic emerged from a poll in Texas, where Dole held a narrow three-point lead over Clinton in what should be one of the most reliable Republican states in the nation.
The president was expected to return to Texas late next week in his bid to become the first Democrat candidate to carry the Lone Star State in 20 years.
Clinton began the day in Atlanta, pushing a proposal to use college students to help teach children to read.

Making a direct appeal to younger voters, Clinton said: "This is your election and we need you. You have most of your tomorrows in front of you. You have your future out there ahead of you, and you have to decide that."

Georgia, home state of House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, was one of four southern states Clinton carried in 1992. He aimed to do better in the region this year and was seen as competitive in at least 10 states.

Dole's speech was a litany of what he said were ethical violations by the Clinton administration, coupled with an angry condemnation of the "liberal media" as well as voters for failing to pay attention.

"We have the president of the United States who won't say he will not pardon somebody who did business with him and might implicate him later on. Where is the outrage in America?" Dole asked, referring to Clinton's refusal to rule out pardons for former Whitewater business partners.

"Where has the media gone in America? ... When will the voters start to focus? ... When do the American people rise up and say, 'Forget the media in America, we're going to make up our minds, you're not going to make up our minds,'" Dole said.
